title: The King and the Barber
summary: A vain royal barber dreams of royal power and schemes to replace Birbal with himself. Birbal assigns the barber a royal task that quickly cures his delusions.
full_text:
The royal barber, Karim, had cut Emperor Akbar's hair and massaged his head with scented almond oil for twelve years. Because the Emperor often made casual conversation during his morning grooming, the barber grew absurdly proud, convincing himself that he understood statecraft far better than the imperial ministers.

One morning, while trimming Akbar's sideburns, Karim remarked: 'Your Majesty, courtiers like Raja Birbal do nothing but talk and make clever jokes, yet they enjoy vast estates! If you gave an ordinary, practical man of the people—such as myself—the position of minister for just one week, I would solve the empire's greatest dilemmas!'

Akbar was amused, but decided to consult Birbal.

When Birbal heard of the barber's ambition, he smiled: 'Sire, let us fulfill his dream tomorrow. Appoint Karim acting minister of the royal stables for one single day.'

Akbar agreed. The next morning, Karim was dressed in embroidered silk robes, given a jeweled turban, and seated in the ministerial pavilion at the royal stables. He puffed out his chest, feeling immensely powerful.

Soon, two burly cavalry officers arrived with two identical white stallions. The officers shouted: 'Minister! These two Arabian stallions were purchased yesterday from a Persian merchant for ten thousand gold mohurs. They look identical, run with identical speed, and have identical markings. But one is four years old, and the other is five years old! We must record their exact ages in the imperial register before noon, or the army treasury will be penalized! Tell us which horse is which!'

Karim stepped forward, sweating in his heavy silk coat. He inspected the horses' ears, stroked their manes, and measured their tails. They looked completely identical! He had no idea what to do. Hours ticked away; the cavalry officers grew impatient and began banging their swords against their shields. The barber began to panic, weeping into his silk sleeves.

Just then, Birbal walked into the stables. Seeing the trembling barber, Birbal asked the grooms to bring a basket of fresh, crunchy sugarcane stalks.

Birbal offered a thick stalk to the first stallion, and another to the second. Both horses munched eagerly. Birbal stepped forward, gently parted their lips, and inspected their teeth:

'Behold,' Birbal showed the officers. 'This stallion has already lost and replaced his corner incisors, which occurs only in a horse's fifth year. This stallion still retains his fourth-year milk corners! The five-year-old is on the right; the four-year-old is on the left.'

The officers cheered and recorded the entries. Karim fell at Birbal's feet, tearing off his ministerial turban: 'Take it back, my lord! I know how to trim hair, but I know nothing of horses or statecraft!'

Birbal helped the humbled barber up, advising him that every honest trade has its honor, but pretending to possess wisdom one has never cultivated leads only to shame.
moral: Those who listen to foolish gossip invite disaster; wisdom tests every whisper.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The King and the Barber"?
options: Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof

By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
